food.text: From 1757 to 1842, during the early to middle Qing dynasty, Guangdong, then known as Canton, was the only port where trade between Chinese and foreign merchants was permitted. The city of Guangzhou has long been a trading hub, and many imported foods and ingredients are used in Cantonese cuisine.

The California Gold Rush (1848–1855) brought 20,000–30,000 immigrants to the US from Canton (Guangdong province), China. Many of them went on to open small restaurants that adapted Chinese food to American customers, and the cooking traced back to this era became American Chinese cuisine.

The street food culture of much of Southeast Asia was established by workers imported from China during the late 19th century. Street food had already become an integral part of Chinese food culture in the 7th century, during the Tang dynasty.

The British Empire and the East India Company succeeded in growing and processing tea in the Indian regions of Darjeeling and Assam. They used an Indian strain of tea as well as Chinese specimens and seeds clandestinely extracted from China by the Scottish botanist Robert Fortune. As a result, Qing China lost its monopoly on tea.

In Canton, Cantonese cooks aimed to serve European tastes in restaurants, which lent an ongoing European influence to Cantonese cuisine. Staples of the European nobility's diet at the time, particularly turtle soup, were available to British merchants and dignitaries visiting Guangdong.
Hotteok, a filled pancake that is now a popular street food in South Korea, originated in Qing dynasty China. It was first brought into Joseon Korea during the 19th century.

By the last quarter of the nineteenth century, big western brands like Lyons, Liptons and Mazawattee dominated the western tea market. By the beginning of the 20th century, Chinese tea was no longer the cash crop it had once been for the Qing empire.

The British taught Cantonese cooks how to make turtle soup. The Caribbean sea turtle typically used in Europe was replaced by the Chinese softshell turtle, giving a European noble dish a local Chinese ingredient.

Two San Francisco restaurants, both founded in 1849, are argued to have been the first Chinese restaurant: the Macau and Woosung restaurant buffet and the Canton Restaurant. Neither has any surviving photographs, so the debate cannot be settled with certainty.
By 1850, there were five Chinese restaurants in San Francisco. Soon afterward, significant amounts of food were being imported from China to America's west coast to supply the growing community.
Chinese merchants in Korea originally sold many kinds of dough snacks, including tang huoshao, jidanbing, tanggao, zhimabing and xianhuabing. Koreans lumped them all together under the name hotteok.

Chinese migrants arrived in Mauritius in the 19th century, mostly Cantonese from Guandong, Hakka from Meixian, and people from Fujian. They are largely credited for making noodles, both steamed and fried, and fried rice popular on the island.

In 1852, the ratio of male to female Chinese immigrants in America was 18:1. Restaurants gave the many bachelors who lacked the resources or knowledge to cook for themselves a connection to home, and served as gathering places and cultural centers.
After Japan conquered Formosa (Taiwan) in 1895, the Japanese developed tea plantations there. They were used in particular to produce British-style black tea for overseas markets.

art.text: In October 1860, during the Second Opium War, some 3,500 British troops set the Old Summer Palace near Beijing ablaze on the orders of Lord Elgin, and the fire lasted three days. Some 300 eunuchs and palace maids who had hidden from the soldiers in locked rooms perished when the complex burned. Only 13 buildings survived intact, and a vast collection of art and historical treasures was destroyed.

Wu Changshuo (1844–1927) was a late Qing calligrapher, painter and seal artist who led the Xiling Seal Art Society of Hangzhou-based seal artists. He did not begin painting until his thirties, later becoming known as a Shanghai School painter for helping to rejuvenate flower-and-bird painting.

Ren Yi, known as Ren Bonian (1840–1896), moved to Shanghai after his father's death in 1855 and became a member of the Shanghai School, which fused popular and traditional painting styles. He ranked among the 'Four Rens' and was noted for his bold brushstrokes and use of color.

Canton porcelain was decorated with enamels in Guangzhou, which was the sole legal port for exporting Chinese goods to Europe before 1842. Its 19th-century famille rose designs typically showed figures, birds, flowers and insects in shades of pink and green.

British High Commissioner Lord Elgin ordered the destruction of the Old Summer Palace on 18 October 1860, in retaliation for the torture of an Anglo-French delegation. Its members had been taken prisoner, confined and tortured in Beijing, and nineteen British, French and Indian captives died as a result of the torture. Parkes and Loch were returned after two weeks, with 14 other survivors. The burning was also a warning to the Qing Empire not to use kidnapping as a political tactic against Britain.

British and French soldiers looting the Old Summer Palace in 1860 preferred porcelain over bronze vessels prized locally for cooking and burial, some dating back some 3,600 years to the Shang, Zhou and Han dynasties. In 1867, Empress Eugénie set up the Chinese Museum at the Palace of Fontainebleau to house the newly acquired treasures.

Between 1884 and 1895, during the reign of the Guangxu Emperor, Empress Dowager Cixi reportedly used up to 22 million silver taels, originally meant to upgrade the Qing navy's Beiyang Fleet, to rebuild the Summer Palace for her 60th birthday. The rebuilt garden was given its present name, Yiheyuan, in 1888.

In 1900, toward the end of the Boxer Rebellion, forces of the Eight-Nation Alliance destroyed the imperial gardens of the Summer Palace and seized many stored artifacts. The palace was restored two years later.

war.text: To pay for Chinese tea, the British began smuggling opium into China, where Chinese citizens became addicted to it. The silver earned from opium sales was then used to buy more tea. The Qing state's attempts to crack down on opium sales eventually led to the Opium Wars, in 1839 to 1842 and 1856 to 1860.

The Qing dynasty's defeat by Britain in the First Opium War ended with the 1842 Treaty of Nanking. Britain, France, the United States, Russia, Germany and Japan later forced China to concede sovereignty and gained territorial, economic and legal privileges. Chinese historians widely include this subjugation in the "century of humiliation."

Historian Edward L. Dreyer argued that China's nineteenth-century humiliations were strongly tied to weakness at sea. At the start of the First Opium War, China had no unified navy, and British naval forces sailed and steamed wherever they wanted to go.

On 14 and 15 August 1900, the Eight-Nation Alliance relieved the siege of the Peking Legation Quarter during the Boxer Rebellion. Boxers and Imperial Chinese Army troops had besieged foreign diplomats, citizens and soldiers there since 20 June 1900. On the night of 13 August the armies, about five miles from the walls, heard heavy artillery and machine-gun fire from inside the city and feared they had arrived one day too late to rescue their countrymen. The assault took on the character of a race to see which national army would win the glory of relieving the Legations first. At the Dongbien gate, an advance Russian force killed 30 Chinese outside, then was caught in a murderous crossfire that killed 26 Russian soldiers and wounded 102.

Although the Qing dynasty failed at sea, its armies did better on land. New but not exactly modern Chinese armies suppressed the midcentury rebellions, maintained control of Xinjiang against Russia, and defeated French forces on land in the Sino-French War.

China's defeat in the Second Opium War (1856-1860) led to more concessions. The 1858 Treaty of Tientsin and the 1860 Convention of Peking required China to legalize opium, pay indemnities, open more ports and the Yangtze River to foreign trade, and let Britain and France establish consulates in Beijing.
In the Second Opium War, the Chinese had no way to stop the 1860 Anglo-French naval expedition from sailing into the Gulf of Zhili. The force landed as near as possible to Beijing.

Historian Jane E. Elliott called it simplistic to say China refused to modernize. She noted that after several defeats China began a massive military modernization in the late 1800s, bought Western weapons, and made its own at arsenals such as the Hanyang Arsenal during the Boxer Rebellion.

The Boxer Rebellion had a second siege three miles from the Legations. The Peitang cathedral had been surrounded by Boxers and the Chinese army since 15 June, defended by 28 foreign priests and nuns, 43 French and Italian soldiers and 3,400 Chinese Catholics. The people sheltering in the Peitang suffered several hundred killed, mostly from starvation, disease and mines detonated beneath the perimeter walls.

The Alliance forces defeated the Chinese army at the Battle of Beicang on 5 August 1900 and the Battle of Yangcun on 6 August. They reached Tongzhou, 14 miles from Beijing, on 12 August. Inside the Legation Quarter, 66 of the 900 foreigners were killed and 150 wounded during the siege. Casualties among the 2,800 destitute Chinese Christians who had taken refuge there with them were not recorded.

On 28 August 1900, foreign armies marched through the Forbidden City to show their complete control of Beijing, a city left battered by the siege, with unburied bodies littering its deserted streets. Chinese authorities protested, but gave way when the armies promised not to occupy it while threatening to destroy it if their passage was disputed.

The peace agreement of 7 September 1901 required China to pay an indemnity of $335 million plus interest over 39 years. It also demanded the execution or exile of government supporters of the Boxers and the destruction of Chinese forts and other defenses in much of northern China. This followed an occupation in which Alliance punitive expeditions in the countryside carried out frequent indiscriminate killings. General Chaffee commented that for every real Boxer killed, fifty harmless coolies or laborers on the farms, including not a few women and children, had been slain.

Gulab Singh's armies conquered Ladakh in 1834. After an unsuccessful campaign into Tibet, Gulab Singh and the Tibetans signed a treaty in 1842 agreeing to stick to the "old, established frontiers," which were left unspecified.

literature.text: After the civil service examination was abolished in 1905, China saw a boom in fiction writing. Literati who had lost their old role struggled to find new social and cultural roles for themselves, and many turned to the novel.

In 1901, Herbert Giles published A History of Chinese Literature, the first survey of its kind to appear in English. Surveys of Chinese literature already existed in Japanese. A large part of the book is given over to translations, letting Chinese authors speak for themselves.

Chinese literature of the Qing dynasty remained mostly unaffected by European influence. The effects of modernization that would lead up to the New Culture Movement became apparent only from the Late Qing period in the 1890s.

Intellectuals looking for solutions outside China's own tradition translated Western expository writing and literature. The translations opened windows onto new, exotic cultures, and the most outstanding were those of Yan Fu (1864–1921) and Lin Shu (1852–1924).

Late Qing fiction shows signs of both the Chinese novelistic tradition and Western narrative modes. It was strikingly concerned with contemporary matters such as social problems, historical upheaval and changing ethical values, which is why it is called modern.
By the end of the Qing dynasty, Chinese culture had entered a new era of written vernacular Chinese for common citizens. Hu Shih and Lu Xun were considered pioneers of modern literature at that time.

Liang Qichao, one of the early writers of science fiction in China, published the 1902 novel The Future of New China. It described potential political reforms for the self-strengthening of China and its development into a world power.

The important novelists of late Qing fiction include Wu Woyao (1866–1910), Li Boyuan (1867–1906), Liu E (1857–1909) and Zeng Pu (1872–1935). Their careers fell in the years when the fiction boom followed the end of the civil service examination.

In 1904, Lin Chuanjia wrote Zhongguo wenxue shi, the first survey of Chinese literature written in Chinese. It followed Giles's English book of 1901 and was inspired by a 1903 translation of Sasakawa's book.

While Europe saw an explosion of novels in the 19th century, China had no counterpart to it. The Ming and early Qing novels remained the pinnacle of classic Chinese fiction, and they are still widely known today through adaptations to opera and other popular forms.

In his preface, Herbert Giles claimed no such history existed even in Chinese, because Chinese scholars saw the "utter hopelessness" of achieving even comparative success in a general survey. He argued that a work inadequate for a native public could still introduce English readers to the field.

The earliest original science fiction in Chinese is believed to be the unfinished novel Lunar Colony, published in 1904 by an unknown author under the pen name Old Fisherman of the Secluded River. The hero Long Menghua flees China with his wife after killing a government official who was harassing his wife's family. Their escape ship is accidentally sunk and his wife disappears. Long is rescued by Otoro Tama, the Japanese inventor of a dirigible, and together with anti-Qing martial artists they rescue her from bandits, then travel to the Moon and establish a new colony.
tags: Old Fisherman of the Secluded River

literature.text: The scholar Lin Yutang complained that Giles's book was a misnomer. He called it a series of attempted essays on certain Chinese works, not even an outline covering the successive periods. Separately, the scholar Qian Zhongshu noted an 'amusing mistake' in Giles's complete version of Ssu-k'ung Tu's twenty-four-stanza philosophical poem.

science.text: After China's defeat in the Second Opium War (1856-1860), the self-strengthening movement developed. It set up arsenals, shipyards, and other facilities, and these became places where China was exposed to foreign scientific knowledge and foreign engineering.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

science.text: China's defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) sparked a "science to save the nation" movement among Chinese intellectuals. The Qing dynasty and later the early Republic of China sent large numbers of students abroad to the United States, Japan, and Europe, many of whom studied engineering and natural sciences.

The self-strengthening movement also helped create state-supported enterprises to develop new economic sectors. Its view of science and technology was summed up in a slogan: "Chinese studies as fundamental, Western learning as useful."
science.source_title: History of science and technology in China

science.text: In 1914, nine Chinese students at Cornell University founded the Science Society. They took the American Association for the Advancement of Science as their organizational model, and became the first comprehensive civil scientific organization in modern China.
tags: American Association for the Advancement of Science

science.text: Marta E. Hanson notes that Western science could not replicate China's millennia-old ceramic and porcelain production techniques until Georges Vogt published his scientific analysis of Chinese porcelain in 1900. It is a reminder of how much Chinese craft knowledge outran Western theory.

The Science Society declared its mission as "advocating science, promoting industry, standardizing terminology, and disseminating knowledge." Its founders included Ren Hongjun, Bing Zhi, Zhao Yuanren, Yang Xingfo, and Guo Tanxian. They founded it because China had no systematic civil scientific organization and no comprehensive periodical for the general public.

politics.text: The Taiping Rebellion (1849–1864) was the first major anti-Manchu movement and posed the most serious threat to Qing rule. During its 14-year course, between 20 and 30 million people died, amid widespread social unrest and worsening famine.

In 1898 the Guangxu Emperor and the scholar Kang Youwei launched extensive reforms during the Hundred Days of Reform, from June 11 to September 21. The reforms threatened the conservative court, so Empress Dowager Cixi took back the throne, put Guangxu under house arrest and abolished the program. She executed six of the reform advisors, including Kang's brother, and called for Kang's arrest and execution.

The Xuantong Emperor, Puyi, abdicated on 12 February 1912 after the Xinhai Revolution, and the Republic of China superseded the Qing dynasty. Historians usually treat this date as the end of the Chinese dynastic system, which had lasted almost four millennia.

Britain's First Opium War of 1839 to 1842 produced the first of the "unequal treaties" imposed on the Qing dynasty. These treaties opened treaty ports, loosened trade restrictions and allowed Christian missionary activity in China.

Hong Xiuquan was a disappointed civil service examination candidate who read the Old Testament in translation and had a series of visions. He announced himself to be the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and in 1851 he established the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom with himself as its king.

Although the Qing tried to keep the traditional tributary system, by the 19th century Qing China had joined a European-style community of sovereign states. Before its downfall it established official diplomatic relations with more than twenty countries, and from the 1870s it set up legations and consulates.

After the Hundred Days of Reform failed, Kang Youwei fled into exile. On 20 July 1899 he and others founded the Chinese Empire Reform Association in Victoria, British Columbia, hoping to unite overseas Chinese, restore the Guangxu Emperor and turn China into a constitutional monarchy.

China's defeats in the Opium Wars (1840–1842, 1856–1860) showed the Celestial Empire that it was no longer a dominant world power. Chinese scholars and political leaders began to study the outside world, and the meaning of the term Celestial Empire was transformed.

Within the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, slavery, concubinage, arranged marriage, opium smoking, footbinding, judicial torture and the worship of idols were all banned. Yet success led to internal feuds, defections and corruption.

British and French troops with modern weapons came to the assistance of the Qing army against the Taiping. Even so, it was not until 1864 that Qing forces under Zeng Guofan succeeded in crushing the revolt.

Throughout the 19th century, western cartographers commonly showed Manchuria, Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet as part of the Chinese Empire, separated from China proper by lines. In the last decade of the Qing dynasty, maps published in China caught up, enclosing these frontiers with fixed international boundaries.

Historian Edward L. Dreyer argued that China's 19th-century humiliations stemmed from weakness at sea. On land the Qing did better: new Chinese armies suppressed the midcentury rebellions, bluffed Russia into a peaceful frontier settlement, and defeated French forces in the Sino-French War (1884–85).

In late 1910, presidents of several provincial assemblies gathered to form what became the first officially registered political party in China. Liang Qichao named it the Imperial Unification Party, and in 1911 it was renamed the Friends of the Constitution Association.

philosophy.text: The academic discipline of philosophy did not enter China until the 19th century. In 1873 the Japanese scholar Nishi Amane first translated the term "philosophy" into Chinese as zhexue, meaning "wisdom learning." He coined it to refer to Western philosophy.

Nishi Amane coined zhexue only for Western philosophy. Yet the argument was that the discipline was in constant flux, which opened the door to a Chinese philosophy. Scholars have debated ever since whether the ancient Chinese masters count as philosophers.

Ancient Chinese education had been based on ethical education. After the Opium War, the educational system was considered an obstruction to realizing Chinese potential. The Dao tong, or Confucian orthodoxy, was refashioned into the "history of Chinese philosophy."

The Rules for Colleges and Universities in 1903 divided academic subjects into disciplines, with classics as one of them. By 1913 the discipline of classical studies was dropped. Before Western importation, China had no divisions of scholarship based on the nature of knowledge.

Chinese intellectuals came to use zongjiao for exclusive systems of thought and practice with a congregational organization distinct from society as a whole. This viewpoint was consistent with the Western post-Enlightenment view of religion.

By 1914, Beijing University had created a Division of Chinese Philosophy. This marked the start of Chinese philosophy as a new academic discipline, in a country where scholarship had never been divided by the nature of knowledge before.

culture.text: Before 1912, China traditionally used a 12-month lunisolar calendar rather than the Gregorian one. Days as well as years were often counted with the 60-part sexagenary cycle, alongside the twelve-year Chinese zodiac. The Gregorian calendar was adopted in 1912.

In imperial China, yellow was the color of the emperor. The flag of the Qing dynasty featured golden yellow as its background. The Plain Yellow Banner and the Bordered Yellow Banner were two of the upper three banners of the Later Jin and Qing dynasty.

Protestant missionary work in China began with the English missionary Robert Morrison in 1807. Missionaries were at first restricted to the Thirteen Factories in Canton and to Macau. Thousands of Protestant men, women and children would eventually live and work in China.

The 1842 treaty ending the First Opium War let missionaries live and work in five coastal cities. In 1860, the treaties ending the Second Opium War opened the whole country. From 50 missionaries in 1860, the number grew to 2,500 in 1900, counting spouses and children.

The Chinese language historically had no overarching term for "religion". The current meaning of zongjiao developed in Chinese discourses around 1900. In its earliest uses, the word referred specifically to Christianity.

After the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, governments and modernizing elites condemned "feudal superstition" and opposed traditional religious practices they believed conflicted with modern values. After the Xinhai Revolution of 1911, most temples were turned to other uses or destroyed, with a few changed into schools. After 1928 the Republic of China's campaign against folk religion temples became more intense in the name of opposing feudal superstition, particularly in north China, and increasingly emphasized the physical destruction of temples.

Female missionaries vehemently opposed footbinding, though male missionaries often saw it as a matter of conscience rather than a sin. In the 1860s, the American Presbyterian Helen Nevius helped combat it by finding Christian husbands for young women with unbound feet. An anti-footbinding organization was founded in Xiamen in 1874.

Li Zongwu, a late Qing intellectual who lived from 1879 to 1943, wrote the Thick Black Theory. It is an exhortation to opportunism. Black itself is generally understood as a neutral color in Chinese culture, though it appears in many negative contexts.

In 1872 in Beijing, the American Methodist Mary Porter banned girls with bound feet from her school. She later became the wife of Boxer Rebellion hero Frank Gamewell. By 1908 the majority of the Chinese elite had spoken out against footbinding, and it was prohibited in 1911.
